name: Self-tanning mousse

lead: Self-tanning mousse is a foam containing dihydroxyacetone (DHA), a sugar-derived compound that darkens the surface of the skin. It gives a bronzed look without sun or sunbeds, developing over hours.

DHA reacts with amino acids in the outermost dead skin cells in a Maillard-type reaction, forming brown pigments called melanoidins. It does not involve melanin or UV. The colour fades over about a week as the surface skin sheds. Dermatology reviews describe DHA as having a generally favourable topical safety record and minimal to no photoprotection.

paras: Users apply it with a mitt, usually after exfoliating, and reapply weekly to keep the colour. It is a common UV-free route to a tan.

Streaks, orange tones and uneven fading are the main reported nuisances. Reviews call for more research on inhalation from sprays and booths, and the colour additive is labeled for external use only. It gives no sun protection, and some studies find sunless-tanner users still use less sun protection.

angle.text: The mousse's DHA reacts with the outer layer of skin to give a bronzed colour that lasts about a week, with no UV exposure. It is a cosmetic colour change; how natural it looks depends on application.

lead: Self-tanning mousse is a foam-format sunless tanner, usually applied with a mitt, that gives the skin a tanned colour without sun or tanning-bed exposure. Its colouring agent is dihydroxyacetone (DHA), a three-carbon sugar. Other sunless tanners come as lotions, gels, sprays, wipes, drops and gradual-tan moisturisers [1][2][3].

People use it to look bronzed, to even out a pale or uneven complexion, or to add colour to the face and body for photos, events or competition. The foam texture spreads quickly and shows where it has been applied, which many users find helps produce an even finish. The colour develops over hours and fades over about a week as the outermost skin cells shed, so it is renewed regularly to keep the look [1][4].

The chain is chemical rather than biological: DHA reacts with amino acids in the dead surface layer of the skin (the stratum corneum) in a Maillard-type browning reaction, forming brown pigments called melanoidins. The process involves neither melanin nor UV radiation [1][5][6][3].

Dermatology reviews describe DHA's topical safety record as generally favourable, state that sunless tanners regulated as cosmetics provide minimal to no photoprotection, and call for more study of inhalation and mucous-membrane exposure, as in spray booths. Studies of sunless tanning as a substitute for UV exposure have produced mixed behavioural findings [2][7][8].
infobox: About 3-5% in consumer products; higher in professional ones [3][4]
Cosmetic; DHA approved as external-use color additive; not for eyes, lips, mucous membranes or inhalation [3][4]

paras: Mousses are whipped, foam-textured sunless tanners. Wikipedia describes consumer DHA products at roughly 3 to 5 percent, with professional products at 5 to 20 percent, and says concentration is adjusted to give lighter or darker shades [3][4]. A patent family dating from 2000 describes a self-tanning mousse composed of a self-tanning agent with a nitrogen-free polymer and nitrogen-free surfactant in a cosmetically acceptable carrier [9][10].

Related products include lotions and gradual-tan moisturisers that build colour with repeated use, sprays and airbrush solutions, and temporary bronzers, which are powders, mousses, gels or lotions that tint the skin and wash off with soap and water; these are often used for one-day colour or to complement a DHA tan [3]. Some formulations pair DHA with erythrulose, a slower-developing sugar; both have been reported to cause contact dermatitis [3].
Grokipedia gives DHA concentrations of about 1 to 15 percent, colour developing in roughly 2 to 4 hours and lasting 3 to 7 days; this is an AI-generated source [1].

DHA is the simplest ketose sugar [4]. Reviews describe it as acting only on the surface of the skin, in the stratum corneum, rather than stimulating the melanin-producing tanning pathway that UV radiation activates through the melanocortin 1 receptor and MITF [1][5][11][12]. Wikipedia describes the reaction as a Maillard reaction with skin keratin, producing melanoidins that can be removed by abrasion, with one pathway being free-radical mediated [3][4]. The Maillard reaction was first described by Louis-Camille Maillard in 1912 and is the same family of browning chemistry seen in cooking [13].

Because the colour depends on skin amino acids and DHA concentration, a Thai study of three DHA creams at 3.5, 4.2 and 5 percent found that colour matching required higher concentrations in darker-skinned volunteers. DHA solutions are described as stable at mildly acidic pH and degrading to a brown product in basic solutions [4].

German scientists recognised DHA as a skin-colouring agent in the 1920s, according to Wikipedia [4]. In the 1950s Eva Wittgenstein at Cincinnati Children's Hospital observed that oral DHA, given as a treatment, stained skin brown on contact [3]. The first commercial DHA self-tanner, Man-Tan, appeared in 1959, followed by Coppertone's Quick Tan in 1960; both gave an orange-toned result that damaged the reputation of early self-tanners [3][4]. Improved formulations and concern about UV tanning helped popularise sunless products in the 1980s, and from the late 1990s automated spray-tan booths broadened the market [3][4]. The FDA listed DHA as an approved cosmetic color additive for external use in the 1970s; Grokipedia gives 1977 [1][4].

The cultural backdrop is the fashion for tanned skin: pale skin signalled high status until the twentieth century, and in 1923 Coco Chanel's tan from Cannes helped make tanning chic, according to Wikipedia; the sunbed followed in 1975 [14]. Public-health concern about UV exposure then pushed interest toward sunless options [3][14].

In appearance communities, self-tanning mousse is one of the common UV-free ways to adopt a tanned look, usually with a mitt. On looksmax.org, a user who applied self-tanner to the face described patchy results, with pale areas around the eyes, mouth and hairline against orange elsewhere, and asked how to fix them before a family event; one reply recommended scrubbing with a sugar or salt scrub to remove colour [15]. Such threads illustrate the most commonly reported frustrations: streaking, missed spots and orange tones [15].
No trial has focused specifically on mousse formulations as opposed to DHA tanners in general. Human studies of DHA and sunless tanning cover behavioural prevention, safety and camouflage uses.

subs.h: Sunless tanning as a substitute for UV exposure
paras: A randomized trial of 250 women on Massachusetts beaches tested a skin cancer prevention intervention that promoted sunless tanning as a substitute for sunbathing [16]. A separate randomized trial examined how UV photographs, photoaging information and use of sunless tanning lotion affected sun protection behaviours [17]. A nationwide representative survey examined users of sunless tanning products and noted a concern that such products may lead people to overestimate their natural skin type and take riskier tanning decisions [8].

The vitiligo camouflage study evaluated DHA as a way to colour-match depigmented patches. Reviews report minimal to no photoprotection from DHA; a 2023 randomized trial reported protection against visible light by DHA in people with erythropoietic protoporphyria [7][18]. Wikipedia reports an SPF of about 3 for DHA colouring [4].
A 2005 Aesthetic Surgery Journal article reviewed spray-on tanning and a 2017 French review covered self-tanning and sunless tanning products [19][20].

The FDA regulates sunless tanners as cosmetics, allows DHA for external use and advises avoiding ingestion, inhalation and contact with eyes, lips and mucous membranes. Spray booth and airbrush application are not approved uses according to a 2018 review [2][7]. Wikipedia notes that booth application may make unapproved exposure difficult to avoid [3][4].

A 2023 review reported irritant and allergic contact dermatitis from DHA, and in-vitro changes in cell function at low millimolar concentrations, while noting that concentrations far higher than those in products were needed for cytotoxicity [7]. Wikipedia reports a 2007 study by Katinka Jung and colleagues in which skin samples treated with 20 percent DHA formed more free radicals in sunlight, a reason sun protection is advised for about 24 hours after application, and a Danish cell-culture study linking DHA to DNA damage; it also notes that the EU's 2010 scientific committee opinion found no risk from spray tanning, which critics said relied on industry-linked unpublished studies [3]. An FDA report is cited as estimating that about 11 percent of applied DHA may penetrate into living skin layers [4]. Because UV photoprotection is not provided, products do not replace sunscreen [2][7].

Wikipedia also notes that tanners containing the sunscreen avobenzone may degrade it in UVA light, and that fragrances and parabens can cause reactions [3][4]. For comparison, UV from indoor tanning is classified by the WHO as a Group 1 carcinogen, and meta-analyses link indoor tanning to higher melanoma risk [14].

Other routes to a tanned look include oral carotenoids such as beta-carotene, lycopene and canthaxanthin, which can colour skin with heavy long-term intake; the FDA has not approved canthaxanthin or tanning pills for this purpose and has warned about them, and canthaxanthin pills have been linked to side effects including retinopathy [3]. Melanotan peptides, developed from University of Arizona research in the 1980s, are sold unlicensed online and have drawn health warnings since 2007 [3]. Tyrosine-based accelerators are marketed for use with UV exposure; Wikipedia says no scientific data support their claims [3].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, self-tanner appears in practical threads about streaks, facial application and product choice; broader claims about safety and sun protection are documented in dermatology reviews [15][7].
